testName: IISER IAT - Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter (Version 2)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Which of the following experimental observations in the photoelectric effect fundamentally contradicted the classical wave theory of light and necessitated the introduction of the quantum (photon) theory?
options: The dependence of saturation current on the intensity of incident light.
The instantaneous emission of photoelectrons regardless of light intensity.
The continuous spread of the energy spectrum of emitted electrons.
questions.explanation: Classical wave theory predicted that energy from a wave is spread evenly over the wavefront. If the light intensity was very low, it would take a measurable amount of time for an electron to accumulate enough energy to escape the metal surface. However, experiments showed that emission is virtually instantaneous (<10⁻⁹ s), proving that energy is delivered in concentrated, discrete packets (photons).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: In a photoelectric experiment, a graph is plotted showing the maximum kinetic energy (K_max) of emitted photoelectrons on the y-axis versus the frequency (ν) of incident light on the x-axis. What does the slope of this straight line uniquely represent?
options: The work function of the metal (Φ)
The ratio of Planck's constant to elementary charge (h/e)
questions.explanation: Einstein's photoelectric equation is K_max = hν - Φ. This takes the linear form y = mx + c, where y = K_max and x = ν. The slope m of the graph corresponds exactly to Planck's constant h.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A photon associated with a monochromatic light beam has an energy of 10 eV. What is the magnitude of its momentum? (Given c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: The momentum p of a photon is given by p = E/c. First, convert energy to Joules: E = 10 eV × (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/eV) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Calculate momentum: p = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁸ / 3 × 10⁸ = 5.33 × 10⁻²⁷ kg·m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron initially at rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. What is its approximate de Broglie wavelength?
questions.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential V is given by the standard formula λ = 12.27 / √V Å. Substituting V = 100 V: λ = 12.27 / 10 = 1.227 Å. Converting Angstroms to nanometers (1 Å = 0.1 nm): λ = 0.1227 nm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Based on this graph, which metal has the higher work function, and what is the ratio of their threshold wavelengths (λ_0X : λ_0Y)?
questions.explanation: The intercept on the frequency axis represents the threshold frequency (ν₀). Metal Y has a higher threshold frequency (2ν₀ vs ν₀), which means it has a higher work function (Φ = hν₀). Threshold wavelength is inversely proportional to threshold frequency (λ₀ = c/ν₀). Ratio λ_0X : λ_0Y = c/ν_0X : c/ν_0Y = ν_0Y : ν_0X = 2ν₀ : ν₀ = 2:1.
questions.imagePrompt: A 2D Cartesian line graph plots Stopping Potential (V_0) on the y-axis against Frequency (ν) on the x-axis. Two straight, parallel, upward-sloping solid lines are shown for two different photosensitive metals, labeled 'Metal X' and 'Metal Y'. The line for Metal X intersects the x-axis at a positive value marked 'ν_0'. The line for Metal Y intersects the x-axis further to the right at a value explicitly marked '2ν_0'.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The work function of a specific metal surface is exactly 4.14 eV. Which of the following incident light wavelengths will successfully cause photoelectric emission from this surface? (Assume hc ≈ 1242 eV·nm)
questions.explanation: The threshold wavelength λ₀ is the absolute maximum wavelength capable of causing emission. λ₀ = hc / Φ = 1242 eV·nm / 4.14 eV = 300 nm. For photoelectric emission to occur, incident wavelength λ must be ≤ 300 nm. Only 250 nm satisfies this.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A proton and an alpha particle are both accelerated from rest through the exact same potential difference V. What is the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to that of the alpha particle (λ_p : λ_α)?
questions.explanation: λ = h / √(2mqV). Since V is constant, λ ∝ 1 / √(mq). For a proton: mass = m, charge = e. λ_p ∝ 1 / √(me). For an alpha particle: mass = 4m, charge = 2e. λ_α ∝ 1 / √((4m)(2e)) = 1 / √(8me) = 1 / (2√2 √(me)). Ratio = (1/1) / (1/2√2) = 2√2 : 1.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: When monochromatic light of wavelength λ illuminates a photosensitive surface, the maximum velocity of the emitted photoelectrons is measured to be v. When the incident wavelength is reduced to λ/2, the maximum velocity is found to be exactly 3v. What is the threshold wavelength (λ₀) of this metallic surface?
questions.explanation: Eq 1: hc/λ - Φ = ½mv². Eq 2: hc/(λ/2) - Φ = ½m(3v)² => 2hc/λ - Φ = 9(½mv²). Substitute Eq 1 into Eq 2: 2hc/λ - Φ = 9(hc/λ - Φ) => 2hc/λ - Φ = 9hc/λ - 9Φ. Rearranging gives 8Φ = 7hc/λ => Φ = 7hc/8λ. Since Φ = hc/λ₀, we equate hc/λ₀ = 7hc/8λ => λ₀ = 8λ/7.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A perfectly reflecting flat mirror of area 10 cm² is illuminated normally by a highly focused 100 W continuous laser beam. What is the total radiation pressure exerted on the mirror surface?
questions.explanation: Radiation force on a perfectly reflecting surface is F = 2P/c = (2 × 100) / (3 × 10⁸) = 6.67 × 10⁻⁷ N. Radiation pressure P_r = F / A. Area A = 10 cm² = 10⁻³ m². P_r = 6.67 × 10⁻⁷ / 10⁻³ = 6.67 × 10⁻⁴ N/m².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Which of the following correctly compares the frequencies (ν) and intensities (I) of the incident light producing curves A and B?
questions.explanation: 1. Stopping potential depends on frequency. A more negative stopping potential means higher max kinetic energy, hence higher frequency. Since -V_0A is more negative than -V_0B, Curve A has higher frequency (ν_A > ν_B). 2. Saturation current depends directly on intensity. Since Curve B reaches a higher saturation level, it represents higher intensity (I_B > I_A).
questions.imagePrompt: A 2D line graph plots Photoelectric Current (i) on the y-axis against Anode Potential (V) on the x-axis. Two distinct saturation curves labeled 'Curve A' and 'Curve B' are shown. Curve A originates from a highly negative stopping potential marked '-V_0A' on the x-axis and levels off at a lower saturation current in the first quadrant. Curve B originates from a less negative stopping potential marked '-V_0B' on the x-axis (closer to the origin than -V_0A) and rises steeply to level off at a significantly higher saturation current than Curve A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: If a beam of thermal neutrons has a characteristic de Broglie wavelength λ at a room temperature of 27°C, at what specific temperature will their average de Broglie wavelength be exactly λ/2?
questions.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength of thermal neutrons is λ = h / √(3mkT), meaning λ ∝ 1 / √T (where T is absolute temperature). To halve the wavelength (λ/2), the temperature must increase by a factor of 4. Initial T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. New T = 300 × 4 = 1200 K. In Celsius, this is 1200 - 273 = 927°C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Photoelectrons are emitted from a metallic surface (work function φ) when illuminated by light of wavelength λ. These electrons subsequently enter a region containing a uniform magnetic field B directed perpendicularly to their velocity. What is the expression for the maximum possible radius R of the circular path they can describe?
questions.explanation: Max kinetic energy is K_max = hc/λ - φ. When a charged particle enters a perpendicular magnetic field, its path radius is R = mv / eB = √(2mK) / eB. Substituting K_max yields R_max = √(2m(hc/λ - φ)) / eB.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question:
Passage: A highly photosensitive metallic plate with a defined work function of 2.0 eV is illuminated by an isotropic monochromatic light source (Power = 1.0 × 10⁻³ W, Wavelength = 310 nm) placed 2.0 m away. The plate has an effective area of 16π × 10⁻⁴ m². Only 1.6% of incident photons yield electrons.

What is the absolute maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons ejected from this metallic plate?
questions.explanation: Energy of a single incident photon E = hc/λ = 1240 eV·nm / 310 nm = 4.0 eV. According to Einstein's equation, K_max = E - φ = 4.0 eV - 2.0 eV = 2.0 eV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Based on the geometry and quantum yield provided in the passage, what is the maximum saturation photocurrent generated in this specific experimental setup?
questions.explanation: Intensity I = P / 4πR² = 10⁻³ / 16π W/m². Power incident on plate P_inc = I × A = (10⁻³ / 16π) × 16π × 10⁻⁴ = 10⁻⁷ W. Photon energy E = 4.0 eV = 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Photons per second = P_inc / E = 1.5625 × 10¹¹. Electrons per second (1.6% yield) = 1.5625 × 10¹¹ × 0.016 = 2.5 × 10⁹. Current i = n × e = 2.5 × 10⁹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ A = 0.4 nA.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The light source is now moved to a new distance of 4.0 m away, and its wavelength is simultaneously altered to 620 nm while maintaining the same 1.0 × 10⁻³ W power output. What is the newly observed stopping potential for the emitted photoelectrons?
questions.explanation: The stopping potential depends strictly on incident photon energy. New photon energy E_new = 1240 / 620 = 2.0 eV. Since E_new is exactly equal to the work function (φ = 2.0 eV), the electrons barely break free with zero kinetic energy (K_max = 0). Thus, no retarding voltage is required, V_stop = 0 V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A rapidly moving electron and a high-energy photon are both observed to possess the exact same de Broglie wavelength λ. What is the mathematical ratio of the kinetic energy of the electron (K_e) to the total energy of the photon (E_ph)?
questions.explanation: Photon energy E_ph = hc/λ. Electron momentum p = h/λ. Non-relativistic electron kinetic energy K_e = p² / 2m = h² / (2mλ²). Ratio K_e / E_ph = (h² / 2mλ²) / (hc / λ) = h / (2mcλ).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Assuming none of the ejected electrons fall back onto the sphere, how many total photoelectrons will be successfully emitted before the emission process completely terminates due to the sphere's own acquired potential?
questions.explanation: Photon energy E = 1240 / 200 = 6.2 eV. Max kinetic energy K_max = 6.2 - 4.2 = 2.0 eV. The isolated sphere loses electrons, acquiring a positive potential. Emission stops when this potential reaches the stopping potential V_0 = 2.0 V. Sphere capacitance C = 4πε₀R. Charge Q = CV = (1 / (9×10⁹)) × (9×10⁻³) × 2.0 = 2.0 × 10⁻¹² C. Number of electrons N = Q/e = (2.0 × 10⁻¹²) / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.25 × 10⁷.
questions.imagePrompt: A schematic diagram depicting an isolated, solid, uncharged metallic sphere resting on a perfectly insulated stand in a hard vacuum environment. The sphere has a radius of exactly 9.0 mm. It is continuously illuminated by a distant ultraviolet light source, represented by wavy arrows labeled with wavelength 'λ'. Small circles with negative signs (representing electrons) are shown escaping from the spherical surface.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A stationary Hydrogen atom is initially excited. Its electron transitions directly from the n=3 state to the n=1 ground state. The photon emitted during this specific quantum transition is directed onto a photosensitive material possessing a work function of 5.1 eV. What is the approximate stopping potential required to halt the fastest photoelectrons emitted from this material?
questions.explanation: Energy levels in H-atom: E_n = -13.6/n² eV. Transition from n=3 to n=1 emits a photon of energy E_ph = -13.6/9 - (-13.6) = 12.09 eV. Using Einstein's equation: K_max = E_ph - Φ = 12.09 eV - 5.1 eV = 6.99 eV. The stopping potential is numerically equal to K_max in eV, yielding 6.99 V ≈ 7.0 V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron (mass m, charge e) is initially at rest at time t=0. A uniform, constant electric field E is suddenly turned on, accelerating the electron. Which of the following expressions correctly represents the instantaneous rate of change of the electron's de Broglie wavelength with respect to time (dλ / dt)?
questions.explanation: Electron acceleration a = eE/m. Velocity v(t) = at = eEt/m. Momentum p(t) = mv(t) = eEt. The de Broglie wavelength λ(t) = h/p(t) = h/(eEt). Taking the time derivative: dλ/dt = d/dt (h * (eE)⁻¹ * t⁻¹) = -h / (eEt²).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A high-energy photon of energy E collides with a perfectly stationary Hydrogen atom in its absolute ground state. The atom absorbs the photon completely and undergoes ionization. The ejected electron escapes and is measured to possess a de Broglie wavelength of exactly 3.32 Å. Determine the incident energy E of the original photon.
questions.explanation: Convert wavelength to kinetic energy using λ ≈ √(150/K) Å. Thus, 3.32 = √(150/K) => 11.02 ≈ 150/K => K ≈ 13.6 eV. The electron escapes with 13.6 eV of kinetic energy. The total energy absorbed must also cover the ionization energy of Hydrogen (13.6 eV). E_photon = Ionization Energy + K_electron = 13.6 eV + 13.6 eV = 27.2 eV.
